turns.content:
hey, can i ask you something? i need to know if i'm being unreasonable here.

yesterday my friend tariq and i went out for burgers to celebrate him finally landing a job after four months of unemployment. i was genuinely happy for him, listened for like 45 minutes about his offer package. then i told him my dad got diagnosed with severe heart disease and is having triple bypass surgery next tuesday. he literally pulled out his phone mid-sentence, chuckled at a fantasy football notification, and said "life is crazy, anyway did i tell you about the gym stipend?" and just... never came back to it.

i left early. now i'm sitting here wondering if i'm overreacting because he was just hyped about the job, or if this is actually as insulting as it feels.

You're not overreacting. That's genuinely hurtful, and I'm sorry — both about your dad, and about getting that response when you finally worked up the moment to share it.

Here's the thing that stands out to me: you gave him 45 minutes of genuine attention on *his* big news. That's what friends do. Then when it was your turn — with something scary and heavy, not even a complaint, just "my dad is having open heart surgery" — he pulled out his phone, laughed at a fantasy football notification, and steered the conversation back to his gym stipend. That's not "he was just excited about the job." Excitement explains talking a lot about the job; it doesn't explain completely stepping over your dad's surgery like it was a speed bump.

The distinction I'd draw: it's not that he failed to have a perfect emotional response. People fumble heavy news all the time — they get awkward, they don't know what to say. But fumbling looks like "oh man, I'm so sorry, is he going to be okay?" even if it's clumsy. What he did was *redirect away from you and back to himself*, mid-sentence, without a single question about your dad. That's a self-centeredness thing, not a nervousness thing.

Leaving early was a reasonable move — better than sitting there seething or blowing up at him.

One thing worth considering before you write him off entirely: some people genuinely don't register that something huge was just said until later. If he reaches out in the next day or two with "hey, I'm sorry, tell me about your dad" — that tells you he's oblivious but not uncaring. If he never brings it up again, or acts like nothing happened, that tells you something too.

Either way, your hurt is proportional to what happened. And how are you doing about your dad? Triple bypass is a lot to carry — do you have other people you can actually lean on right now?

yeah... you're right that i need to think about what i wanted from telling him. i think i just wanted him to hear it. like not even fix it or say the perfect thing. just... not laugh at his phone and move on.

also about my dad—i haven't really told many people yet. it's still sinking in. tuesday feels so soon.

That's such a clear, simple thing to want — just to be heard. Not comforted perfectly, not fixed. Just "oh man, that's heavy, how are you doing?" It costs nothing, and he couldn't do it for ten seconds. Wanting that doesn't make you needy; it makes you a person who showed up for a friend and hoped he'd do the same.

And it makes sense that you haven't told many people yet. Saying it out loud makes it more real, and part of you probably wants to keep it in the "still processing" stage a little longer. There's no deadline on that. You told Tariq because it was bursting out of you — that's usually a sign it's time to let a few more people in, but at your pace, and with people who've earned it.

Tuesday feeling soon — that's because it is soon. A week is nothing when you're wrapping your head around your dad's heart being worked on. A couple of honest things that might help, take or leave:

- **It's okay to be scared even though bypass surgery is common and surgeons do these constantly.** Statistics are cold comfort when it's *your* dad on the table. Both things can be true: it's a routine, well-practiced procedure AND it's terrifying. You don't have to pick one.
- **The waiting is often worse than the day itself.** Surgery days have a strange momentum — you get there, things happen, the surgical team updates you. It's these days *before*, with nothing to do but think, that tend to be the hardest.
- **You don't have to be strong at the hospital.** If you've got a sibling, your mom, an aunt, anyone — being scared together is easier than being scared politely.

Is there anyone in your life who's shown up for you before, who you could tell this week? Even just one person who'll sit with you Tuesday? And is there anything I can help with — like questions to ask the surgical team, or what recovery usually looks like after triple bypass, if knowing more would help it feel less unknown?

yeah i think i just wanted... i don't know, the basic thing. the "oh shit, is your dad okay?" that costs zero effort. and he couldn't even do that.

tuesday feels surreal. like i keep thinking about what i'll do that morning. just sit in a waiting room for hours i guess. feels weird to be more upset about tariq than about the surgery right now but maybe that's just easier to focus on.

That last thing you said — that's a really perceptive observation, and I think you've nailed it. Being more upset about Tariq than the surgery isn't weird at all. It's that the Tariq thing is *solvable-feeling* anger: someone did a clear wrong, you can be mad about it, it has a shape. Your dad's surgery has no villain, no fix, nothing to do but wait. So the brain parks itself on the thing it can actually chew on. Classic displacement, and honestly kind of healthy — it's your mind pacing in the room it can move around in.

Also, the Tariq thing isn't really separate from the surgery. He failed you at the exact moment the fear was leaking out. Of course it stings more than usual — you handed him the scariest thing you're carrying and he handed you back a gym stipend. The hurt and the fear are tangled together.

On Tuesday morning, a few thoughts:

- **You don't have to perform calm in that waiting room.** Bring someone if you can, or bring a distraction — a downloaded show, a game, whatever. Nobody's watching you to see if you're grieving correctly.
- **Hospitals usually have a liaison or the surgical team gives periodic updates.** You won't be totally in the dark for hours — someone will come out at milestones (anesthesia done, grafts done, closing up). Knowing there are checkpoints can make the wait feel less like a void.
- **Eat something that morning.** Sounds dumb, but people forget, and a body running on no sleep and no food makes waiting about 40% worse.

And for what it's worth — the fact that you're this reflective while carrying all this says you're handling it better than you're giving yourself credit for.

Do you know yet if you'll be at the hospital alone, or will family be there? And have you decided anything about Tariq — whether you'll say something to him or just let it sit for now?

i think i might send him a message tonight. not a long angry one, just something like "hey man, i told you my dad is having heart surgery next week and you pulled out your phone and changed the subject. that hurt. i need some space." is that too much?

That's not too much at all — it's actually a really solid message. Short, factual, no insults, states the impact, states what you need. You're not calling him a bad friend or demanding an apology; you're just telling him what happened and what you're doing about it. That's about as fair as a hurt message gets.

A couple of small thoughts if you want them:

- **Your draft is good as-is.** Don't let it grow into a longer one tonight. Length tends to invite debate ("that's not how it happened, I did ask about your dad") rather than reflection. Short and specific is harder to argue with.
- **One tiny tweak to consider:** "i need some space" is doing a lot of work — it's clear and fair. If you want to leave a door open, you could add something like "i'm dealing with a lot right now and i couldn't just let it slide." But you also don't owe him an explanation or a softened landing. He's the one who dropped the ball.
- **Send it whenever you're ready, but know you don't have to send it tonight.** There's no deadline on this. If sending it before Tuesday feels like one more thing on your plate, it can wait until after. Your bandwidth belongs to your dad this week.

One thing to brace for, gently: he might respond defensively at first ("dude i was just excited, chill"), and that response will tell you a lot. Someone who values you usually circles back within a day — "okay yeah, i'm sorry, that was shitty of me. how's your dad?" Someone who argues with you for being hurt is confirming the original problem.

Whatever he says back, you did your part: you were honest, you didn't explode, you asked for space. The rest is his to figure out.

And seriously — how are you feeling about Tuesday now that it's a few days out? Have you figured out the logistics of the morning yet?

yeah you're right. short and specific is harder to argue with. i think i'll send it tonight just to get it off my chest before tuesday.

what if he just says "ok" and never brings it up again though? i think that would hurt worse than him getting defensive honestly.

Yeah, I get why that scenario feels worse — defensiveness at least means he *felt* something. "Ok" would mean your hurt registered as a minor administrative note. That's a lonely image.

But here's the reframe that might help: **"ok" is an answer too, just a quiet one.** If he reads "you hurt me, my dad's having open heart surgery, I need space" and responds with "ok" and never follows up — that's not ambiguity you have to agonize over. That's a complete, unambiguous data point about what he's willing to give. It would hurt, genuinely, but it would also free you. No more wondering if you're being too sensitive, no more auditing the friendship for signs it's still alive. The question would be answered.

And honestly? The odds of that specific outcome are lower than your anxiety is telling you. People who don't care at all usually don't get 45 minutes of listening about their job offer — self-centered people still tend to respond when directly confronted with "you hurt me." The more likely bad outcomes are defensiveness or a half-apology ("sorry man, rough week"), and even those often ripen into real apologies a day or two later once the embarrassment fades.

One more thing worth holding onto: **his response measures him, not you.** You're not sending this message to get a specific reply — you're sending it because it's true and you deserve to have said it. Whatever comes back, you'll have been honest and dignified about it. That part doesn't change based on what he does with it.

And if the worst case happens and it stings — you come back here and vent about it. That's allowed.

Send it tonight if it feels right, then close the tab and do something for yourself. You've got a big week ahead, and the Tariq file can stay closed until you decide to open it again. How are you feeling about it now — more settled, or still churning?
